title: Learn by Doing: Module One
lead: Sit Module One as a paper: fifty objective questions, then the three theory questions with their practicals, each answered twice, once as you would write it and once taught from nothing.
intro:
This is Module One sat as a paper, not read as a lesson. It is the module your Question 1 comes from, and Question 1 is one of the two you will write.

How to sit it

Part A, fifty objective questions. All thirty of Test 1 come first, because Test 1 was Module One from end to end and this examiner reuses his own questions. Then twenty more, chosen so that between them the fifty touch as many separate facts as fifty questions can. Answer, read the verdict, move on.

Part B, three theory questions, each with a practical, which is the shape the lecturer confirmed. For each one: read the scenario, write your full answer in your book, and only then open Part 1, the answer as you would write it in the hall. Part 2 then teaches the same question from nothing, in steps, for the parts you could not write.

If you are short of time, do Part B first. Fifty objective questions are worth fifty marks between three modules; one theory question is worth 17.5 on its own.

questions.heading: The SDLC phases, and a retail company that keeps changing its mind

scenario.tag: Course text, Module One Unit 2, pages 25 and 26
scenario.text:
1. Explain the Planning and Analysis phases of the System Development Life Cycle (SDLC), highlighting their objectives and key activities.
2. A medium-sized retail company wants to develop a new online sales and inventory management system. The company expects frequent changes in customer requirements, plans to introduce new features regularly, and seeks continuous user feedback throughout development. As a systems analyst,
a) Identify the most suitable software development approach for this project.
b) Justify your choice by explaining how the selected approach addresses the company’s needs.
c) Outline the key activities that would be carried out using this approach during system development.

questions.asked:
This is the course text's own assignment, and it is already in the shape the lecturer confirmed: a theory part, then a practical scenario. Answer it as a 17.5 mark question.

PartWhat to writeMarks
(a)The Planning and the Analysis phases: the objective of each, and the activities of each8
(b i)Identify the most suitable approach for the retail company1.5
(b ii)Justify the choice against what the company actually said it needs5
(b iii)Outline the key activities that would be carried out3

breakdown.question: Before you write: what are the two halves of this question worth separately, what single phrase in the scenario decides the answer, and what would earn nothing?
breakdown.answer:
Given A medium-sized retail company, an online sales and inventory system, and three stated needs: frequent requirement changes, new features regularly, continuous user feedback.

Asked Two separate things. A bookwork half on two SDLC phases, which you either know or do not. Then a judgement half: name an approach, defend it, and say what the work would look like.

The deciding phrase "expects frequent changes in customer requirements". That single clause rules out every predictive method, because a predictive approach defines requirements upfront and has limited flexibility to accommodate changes.

Worth nothing Writing the word Agile and stopping. The identify part is 1.5 of 17.5. The marks are in tying each of the company's three phrases to a feature of the approach.

exam.problem: (a) Explain the Planning and Analysis phases of the SDLC, their objectives and key activities. (b) For the retail company that expects frequent requirement changes, regular new features and continuous user feedback: identify the most suitable approach, justify it, and outline the key activities.
exam.answer:
(a) The Planning phase.

Objective: to identify the scope of the new system, to ensure the project is feasible, and to develop a schedule, a resource plan and a budget.

Its five activities:

  1. Define the problem.
  2. Produce the project schedule.
  3. Confirm project feasibility.
  4. Staff the project.
  5. Launch the project.

Feasibility is confirmed here, in Planning, and not in Analysis. It comes in five kinds: economic (a cost and benefit analysis), organisational, technical (are the technology and skills available), resource, and schedule (can it be done in the time available).

Deliverables: the project proposal and recommendation, the investigation report, an analysis of alternatives, a cost and benefit analysis, and the schedule.

The Analysis phase.

Objective: to understand and document the business needs and the processing requirements of the new system. Analysis is essentially a process of discovery and understanding: it establishes WHAT the system must do, never HOW it will do it, which is Design's question.

Its six activities:

  1. Gather information.
  2. Define the system requirements.
  3. Prioritise the requirements.
  4. Build a prototype model for discovery.
  5. Generate and evaluate alternatives.
  6. Review the recommendations with management.

Information is gathered by observing users at work, interviewing them, reading existing documents on procedures, business rules and job responsibilities, and reviewing the existing automated systems.

Deliverables: the detailed system requirements, a revised cost and benefit analysis, and a revised schedule.

(b i) The approach: an adaptive, iterative and incremental approach, that is Agile. Agile development, in a method such as Scrum, is the most suitable approach for this project. Where the examiner will accept a near neighbour: RAD or system prototyping, for the same reasons, since all three are adaptive.

(b ii) The justification, taking the company's own words one at a time.

What the company saysWhat the approach does about it
"expects frequent changes in customer requirements"An adaptive approach lets requirements evolve over time, and only the requirements chosen for the current iteration are analysed and designed in detail. A predictive approach would fix them upfront and has limited flexibility to accommodate change.
"plans to introduce new features regularly"Development is iterative and incremental: every iteration is a complete small project that ends in a working, testable increment, so a new feature is simply the next increment rather than a change request against a finished design.
"seeks continuous user feedback throughout development"Agile rests on strong user involvement and collaboration, and each sprint ends in a sprint review where the working increment is shown to the user and the feedback is taken into the next sprint.
Online sales and inventory, a competitive marketWorking software is valued over extensive documentation, so useful function reaches the business early instead of at the end of a long sequence.

The alternative I reject, and why. Waterfall is unsuitable here: it demands that requirements are clear and stable throughout, it is difficult to respond to changes, and it gives the customer little opportunity to preview the system until it may be too late. Every one of those collides with a sentence in the scenario.

(b iii) The key activities that would be carried out.

  1. Initiation and requirements planning. Establish the high-level scope, the business problem, the objectives, the key stakeholders and the major features. Requirements are deliberately not fully specified: they are captured at a high level as user stories and prioritised by business value and urgency.
  2. Sprint planning and task assignment. The team selects the highest priority user stories it can complete in a short, time-boxed sprint and assigns the tasks.
  3. Iterative analysis and design. Only the requirements selected for this sprint are analysed and designed in detail.
  4. Development and testing within the sprint. The increment is built and tested inside the sprint, with continuous testing and quality assurance rather than one test phase at the end, so defects are found early.
  5. Sprint review and retrospective. The working increment is demonstrated to the retail company's users, their feedback becomes new or reprioritised stories, and the team improves its own process before the next sprint.
  6. Repeat until the sponsor and users agree the system has enough functionality to be installed, then convert and train.

frames.teach: Start with the thing the whole course hangs on. A system is not built in one go: it is built in a fixed order of phases, and that order is called the System Development Life Cycle, the SDLC.
frames.ask: Guess the order for building anything at all, a house included. What has to happen first, and what has to happen last?

frames.check: Plan it, work out what it must do, design it, build it, then keep it running.
frames.teach: That is the SDLC, in the manual's five names: Planning, Analysis, Design, Implementation, Support. One word each: Planning asks SHOULD WE. Analysis asks WHAT. Design asks HOW. Implementation builds it and switches over. Support keeps it alive for years.
frames.ask: A question asks which phase decides whether the project is worth doing at all. Which one, and what is that decision called?

frames.check: Planning, and the decision is feasibility.
frames.teach: Feasibility belongs to Planning. That is examined constantly, because it sounds like analysis and is not. Five kinds: economic, organisational, technical, resource, schedule. Planning's five activities: define the problem, produce the schedule, confirm feasibility, staff the project, launch the project.
frames.ask: So what is left for Analysis to do, if the problem has already been defined in Planning?

frames.check: Work out in detail what the system must do.
frames.teach: Analysis is discovery and understanding. Its objective is to understand and document the business needs and processing requirements. Six activities: gather information, define requirements, prioritise requirements, build a prototype for discovery, generate and evaluate alternatives, review recommendations with management.
frames.ask: One sentence that separates Analysis from Design, and wins a mark every time you write it.

frames.check: Analysis says WHAT the system must do; Design says HOW it will do it.
frames.teach: That is the bookwork half done. Now the practical half. Every practical in Module One is the same shape, because Module One has no diagrams: a scenario, and a judgement you must justify. Identify, justify, outline.
frames.ask: In the retail scenario, which single phrase tells you the requirements will NOT stay still?

frames.check: "expects frequent changes in customer requirements".
frames.teach: That phrase decides the question. Methods split into two families. Predictive: requirements defined upfront, linear and structured sequence, heavy documentation, limited flexibility for change. Adaptive: requirements evolve, iterative and incremental, strong user involvement, working systems over documentation.
frames.ask: Which family does the retail company need, and name one method in it?

frames.check: Adaptive: Agile, or RAD, or system prototyping.
frames.teach: Agile is a group of methods where every iteration is a complete software project, run in short time-boxed sprints. Its four activities are the ones to quote: create and prioritise user stories, sprint planning and task assignment, development and testing within the sprint, sprint review and retrospective.
frames.ask: You have now named Agile. Out of 17.5 marks, how much is that worth?

frames.check: About 1.5. Naming it earns almost nothing.
frames.teach: The marks live in part (b ii). Quote the company's phrase, then answer it with a feature: "frequent changes" answered by requirements that evolve iteration by iteration; "new features regularly" answered by each iteration delivering a working increment; "continuous feedback" answered by the sprint review.
frames.ask: One habit is left, worth the last mark on any methodology question. What have you not done yet?

frames.check: Named the alternative you rejected, and why.
frames.teach: Close with it: "Waterfall was rejected: it requires requirements to be clear and stable throughout, it is difficult to respond to change, and it gives the customer little opportunity to preview the system until it may be too late." That sentence shows the examiner the judgement he is testing, and it is two lines long.

questions.heading: Waterfall, its variants, and a payroll the auditors will read

scenario.tag: written for practice, in the shape the lecturer confirmed
scenario.text: A State Ministry of Education wants to replace the paper based payroll that pays its twelve thousand teachers. The rules for salary, tax and pension deductions are fixed by statute and published in a circular, and they will not change during the project. The Auditor General must be able to trace how every figure was calculated, and the Ministry insists that full documentation be handed over at the end. The system runs once a month, in a single batch. There is no pressure to deliver early: the target is the beginning of the next financial year. The development team is a group of newly recruited graduate trainees, and some of them are expected to be posted elsewhere before the project ends.

questions.asked:
PartWhat to writeMarks
(a)State four advantages and six disadvantages of the Waterfall model, and the conditions under which the course text says it should be used7
(b i)Identify the most suitable methodology for the Ministry, and the variant of it you would use2.5
(b ii)Justify both choices against what the scenario actually says5
(b iii)Outline how you would carry out the changeover from the old payroll to the new one, and why that way3

breakdown.question: Five clauses in that scenario each point at the same answer. Find as many as you can before you read on, and say which phase the changeover question belongs to.
breakdown.answer:
The clauses Rules fixed by statute and will not change (stable requirements). Auditor must trace every figure (documentation and control). Full documentation handed over (documentation again). Runs once a month in a single batch (a transaction oriented batch system, the manual's own first condition for Waterfall). No pressure to deliver early. A team of trainees who may leave (the manual's surprising seventh condition).

Asked Bookwork on Waterfall, then a judgement with a variant named, then a conversion decision.

The changeover belongs to the Implementation phase, and the word for it is conversion or installation.

The trap Everything you have practised says adaptive and Agile. This scenario is the opposite case, and the examiner sets both.

exam.problem: (a) Four advantages, six disadvantages and the conditions for using Waterfall. (b) For a statutory teacher payroll with fixed rules, an audit trail, a batch run, no time pressure and a changing team of trainees: identify the methodology and variant, justify both, and outline the changeover.
exam.answer:
(a) The Waterfall model. A predictive methodology in which the phases are carried out in strict sequence, each finished and signed off before the next begins.

Four advantages:

  1. It is easy to understand and easy to use.
  2. It provides structure to inexperienced staff.
  3. Its sequential approach and strict controls ensure adequate documentation and design reviews, which gives quality, reliability and maintainability.
  4. The progress of development is measurable.

Six disadvantages:

  1. It is inflexible, slow, costly and cumbersome, because of its significant structure and tight controls.
  2. Forward only progress, with slight backward movement, gives a false impression of progress.
  3. There is little opportunity for the customer to preview the system, until it may be too late.
  4. Problems are often not discovered until system testing.
  5. It is difficult to respond to changes.
  6. It produces excessive documentation, which is time consuming to keep updated.

When the course text says to use it, seven conditions: the system is transaction oriented and batch; the project is large, expensive and complicated; the objectives are clear and the solution is known; there is no pressure for immediate implementation; the requirements are clear and comprehensive; the requirements are stable throughout; and the team is inexperienced or may change during implementation. The project types named are government systems, financial applications, and regulatory or safety critical systems.

(b i) The methodology: Waterfall, in its V-shape variant.

(b ii) The justification, clause by clause.

What the scenario saysThe condition it satisfies
Salary, tax and pension rules fixed by statute, and will not changeRequirements clear, comprehensive and stable throughout, which is the condition Waterfall lives or dies by
It is a government payroll, run for a MinistryThe text names government systems and financial applications as Waterfall's own project types
Runs once a month in a single batchA transaction oriented batch system, the first condition listed
No pressure to deliver earlyNo pressure for immediate implementation
The Auditor General must trace every figure, and full documentation is handed overWaterfall's strict controls ensure adequate documentation and design reviews
Graduate trainees, some of whom will be posted awayIt provides structure to inexperienced staff, and it suits a team that may change during implementation, because the documentation carries the knowledge when the people leave

Why the V-shape variant in particular. V stands for verification and validation. It keeps the sequential structure but sets a direct relationship between each development phase and its corresponding testing phase: development goes down the left of the V, testing comes up the right, so verification and validation are built in from the beginning instead of deferred to the end. The text says to use the V-model when the system requires high reliability, when all requirements are known up front, and when the solution and the technology are known. A payroll that pays twelve thousand teachers and answers to an auditor is exactly that system, and the V-model's early test plans answer Waterfall's own weakness, that problems are often not discovered until system testing.

The alternative I reject. Agile: the requirements cannot evolve, because they are set by statute; and Agile deliberately eliminates the documentation overhead that this project is contractually required to deliver.

(b iii) The changeover. Conversion, or installation, is an Implementation activity: the process of turning off the old system and turning on the new one. There are four approaches: direct cutover, parallel, phased and pilot.

For this payroll I would use parallel conversion, running the old payroll and the new one side by side for a month or two until it is clear the new one has no bugs. It is the most expensive approach, because everything is done twice, and it is the safest, which is the right trade when the cost of a wrong figure is a teacher not paid and an audit query. Direct cutover is rejected: it is the cheapest and fastest and the most dangerous, because there is no fallback. Running both also gives the auditor two sets of figures to compare, which is the evidence the trace requires.

Whichever approach is chosen, one of the most important aspects of conversion is developing a training plan to teach users the new system and help manage the change it introduces.

frames.teach: A methodology is the standard process you follow to build the system: which phases, in what order, and how much you write down. The first choice a project manager makes is which one, and the course text is blunt that no one methodology is always best.
frames.ask: If requirements can never change, would you rather plan everything once at the start, or plan a little and keep adjusting?

frames.check: Plan everything once. There is nothing to adjust to.
frames.teach: That is the predictive family, and its oldest member is Waterfall: the phases in strict sequence, each finished before the next starts. Its strength is control. Its weakness is that it cannot bend.
frames.ask: Name two things you gain from doing it in that order, before reading on.

frames.check: Structure and documentation, so progress can be measured.
frames.teach: The four advantages to quote: easy to understand and use; provides structure to inexperienced staff; strict controls ensure adequate documentation and design reviews, giving quality, reliability and maintainability; and progress is measurable.
frames.ask: Now the other side. What is the danger of a method where you cannot go back?

frames.check: A mistake made early is only discovered at the end.
frames.teach: Exactly two of the six disadvantages: problems are often not discovered until system testing, and there is little opportunity for the customer to preview the system until it may be too late. The others: inflexible, slow, costly and cumbersome; forward only progress gives a false impression of progress; difficult to respond to changes; excessive documentation.
frames.ask: Six conditions for using Waterfall are easy to guess from that list. The seventh is not. What might it be?

frames.check: The team is inexperienced, or may change during implementation.
frames.teach: That surprises people. The reason is that the documentation carries the knowledge, so the method survives people leaving. The other six: transaction oriented batch system; large, expensive, complicated; clear objectives and known solution; no pressure for immediate implementation; requirements clear and comprehensive; requirements stable.
frames.ask: Read the Ministry scenario again. How many of the seven does it satisfy?

frames.check: Six of them, in six separate sentences.
frames.teach: That is how this examiner writes a scenario: one clause per condition. Your justification does the same in reverse, quoting the clause and naming the condition it satisfies. Say six things briefly, not one thing at length.
frames.ask: Waterfall has two variants. One of them exists to fix the testing weakness. Which, and what do its two letters stand for?

frames.check: The V-shape model. V is for verification and validation.
frames.teach: Development goes DOWN the left of the V, testing comes UP the right, each phase paired with its test phase. Use it when reliability is high stakes, all requirements are known up front, and the solution and technology are known. The other variant is the parallel model, which splits the system into subprojects AFTER general analysis and high level design, to save time.
frames.ask: Last part. The old payroll is running and the new one is ready. Name the four ways to switch over.

frames.check: Direct cutover, parallel, phased and pilot.
frames.teach: Direct is cheapest, fastest and most dangerous, with no fallback. Parallel runs both for a month or two: safest and most expensive. Phased replaces parts of the system; pilot gives it to a few users first. Phased splits the system, pilot splits the users, and that pair is confused constantly.
frames.ask: For a payroll answering to an auditor, which one, and in one clause, why?

frames.check: Parallel, because a wrong figure means a teacher goes unpaid, so the extra cost buys a fallback and two sets of figures to compare.
frames.teach: Finish by naming the phase the question belongs to: conversion is an Implementation activity, and the most important part of it is the training plan that teaches users the new system and manages the change. Naming the phase costs one line and shows the examiner you know where you are standing.

questions.heading: The analyst, feasibility, and a microfinance bank with a problem

scenario.tag: written for practice, in the shape the lecturer confirmed
scenario.text: A microfinance bank with eleven branches tracks its loans on spreadsheets. Each branch keeps its own copy, and head office only learns that a loan has gone bad when the branch manager telephones. The Managing Director wants a system that shows every outstanding loan across all branches, flags a repayment the day it is missed, and produces the returns the regulator requires each quarter. She has asked you, as the systems analyst, to take the project from idea to installation. The branch managers are willing to be involved but say they cannot be away from their desks for long. The bank has a small IT unit that already runs its accounting package.

questions.asked:
PartWhat to writeMarks
(a)Who a systems analyst is, the seven roles and responsibilities, and which kind of skill the course text calls the most important, with the reasons it gives7
(b i)Apply the analyst's problem solving approach to this bank: state what you would actually do at each step6
(b ii)State which feasibility studies you would carry out, what each would examine here, and which phase they belong to4.5

breakdown.question: Part (b i) says apply, not list. What is the difference worth, and what does the phrase about branch managers who cannot leave their desks tell you to do later in the answer?
breakdown.answer:
List against apply A list of the eight steps is bookwork, and half marks at best. Applying means each step names something in THIS bank: the spreadsheets, the eleven branches, the missed repayment, the regulator's quarterly return.

The branch managers They are your source of requirements and they have little time. That points at the fact finding techniques that cost the user least: questionnaires and sampling existing documentation, with short interviews rather than long ones.

Given A real business problem stated in business terms, which is what step 1 is about: who is involved, what business processes come into play, and what other systems would be affected.

Watch The other system that would be affected is the accounting package the IT unit already runs.

exam.problem: (a) Who is a systems analyst, the seven roles, and the most important skill with reasons. (b) For a microfinance bank moving eleven branches off spreadsheets: apply the analyst's problem solving approach step by step, and state the feasibility studies you would carry out and the phase they belong to.
exam.answer:
(a) Who the analyst is. A systems analyst is the professional who studies an organisation's existing system to identify its problems and requirements, and who then recommends and helps deliver improvements. The analyst is a translator in three directions: business objectives into functional requirements, user needs into system specifications, and technical jargon into terms non technical people understand.

The seven roles and responsibilities:

RoleWhat it involves
Requirements analysisGathers, analyses and documents user and system requirements using structured techniques
System evaluationStudies existing systems to identify problems, inefficiencies and areas for improvement
Feasibility studiesAssesses technical, economic, operational, legal and schedule feasibility
System modelling and documentationPrepares models such as DFDs, use case diagrams and ERDs
Liaison roleHandles communication between stakeholders to ensure mutual understanding
Solution recommendationProposes solutions including hardware, software and process improvements
Support during development and implementationAssists in design, testing, user training and deployment

The most important skill. The analyst needs technical, business and people knowledge, but the course text is explicit that interpersonal skills are the analyst's most important skills. Two reasons are given: analysts rely on managers, users, programmers, technical specialists, customers and vendors to take a system from idea to implementation; and people are the source of requirements information, the labour that builds systems, and the ultimate users of it.

(b i) The analyst's problem solving approach, applied to this bank.

  1. Research and understand the problem. Establish who is involved (the branch managers, head office credit control, the MD, the regulator), what business processes come into play (loan disbursement, repayment collection, bad debt reporting, quarterly regulatory returns), and what other systems would be affected (the accounting package the IT unit already runs). The problem is not "they use spreadsheets": it is that head office cannot see an outstanding loan until someone telephones.
  2. Verify that the benefits of solving it outweigh the costs. Set the cost of the new system against the money now lost to late detection of bad loans and the cost of compiling returns by hand from eleven files.
  3. Define the requirements for solving it. A single consolidated loan register across the eleven branches; automatic flagging of a repayment on the day it is missed; the regulator's quarterly return produced from the same data.
  4. Develop a set of possible solutions. Extend the existing accounting package; buy a packaged microfinance system; build a new system. Three alternatives, so there is something to choose between.
  5. Decide which is best and make a recommendation. The challenge is to select the solution with the fewest risks and the most benefits, and to recommend it to the MD with the reasoning shown.
  6. Define the details of the chosen solution. The design specifications: databases, networks, program modules, operating procedures, user interfaces and conversion plans.
  7. Implement the solution. Build and test it, convert the eleven spreadsheets into the new database, train the branch managers, and install it.
  8. Monitor to make sure the desired results are obtained. Check after a quarter that missed repayments really are flagged on the day, and that the regulator's return comes out of the system rather than out of a spreadsheet.

A note on gathering the requirements here. The branch managers cannot leave their desks for long, so I would lean on the techniques that cost the user least time: sampling the existing documentation, that is the spreadsheets and the returns already filed, and questionnaires to all eleven branches, reserving interviews for the credit control staff at head office.

(b ii) Feasibility. Feasibility is confirmed in the Planning phase, not in Analysis. The course text gives five kinds, and for this bank each asks a different question:

KindWhat it examines here
EconomicA cost and benefit analysis: does the value of catching bad loans early and of automated returns exceed the cost of building and running the system
OrganisationalWill eleven branch managers accept a system that makes their loan book visible to head office daily, and does it fit how the bank is run
TechnicalAre the technology and the skills available: a small IT unit that runs an accounting package can maintain a system, but perhaps not build one
ResourceAre the people, the money and the equipment available for the length of the project, including branch managers' time
ScheduleCan it be done before the next quarterly return is due

Where a question's wording is closer to the other list the text gives, use that one instead: technical, economic, operational, legal and schedule. Both lists appear in the course text.

frames.teach: Before any method or diagram, the course text asks a simpler question: what is this job? A systems analyst studies an existing system, finds its problems and requirements, and recommends improvements.
frames.ask: A bank keeps its loans on spreadsheets and head office finds out about a bad loan by telephone. In one sentence, what is the actual problem?

frames.check: Head office cannot see an outstanding loan until someone tells them.
frames.teach: Notice what you did NOT say: "they use spreadsheets". Stating the problem in business terms rather than technology terms is the analyst's first move, and it is step 1 of eight.
frames.ask: Step 1 is research and understand the problem. The text names three things you must establish. Guess one.

frames.check: Who is involved; what business processes come into play; what other systems would be affected.
frames.teach: Those three are asked for by name in questions, so learn them as a set. In this bank: the branch managers and head office; loan disbursement, repayment and regulatory reporting; and the accounting package the IT unit already runs.
frames.ask: Step 2 comes before defining any requirement, and stops many projects dead. What would you check second?

frames.check: That the benefits of solving it outweigh the costs.
frames.teach: Then: 3 define the requirements, 4 develop a set of possible solutions, 5 decide which is best and recommend it, 6 define the details, 7 implement, 8 monitor to make sure you obtain the desired results. Eight steps, in that order.
frames.ask: At step 5, what does the text say makes one alternative better than another?

frames.check: The fewest risks and the most benefits.
frames.teach: Quote that phrase. Now the other half of the question. The analyst needs three kinds of knowledge: technical, business and people. The ranking is examined, and it is not the one most students expect.
frames.ask: Which of the three does the course text call the most important, and why would that be?

frames.check: Interpersonal, that is people skills.
frames.teach: The reasons are given, so give them: analysts depend on managers, users, programmers, technical specialists, customers and vendors to take a system from idea to implementation; and people are the source of requirements, the labour that builds the system, and its ultimate users.
frames.ask: Now feasibility. Which SDLC phase confirms it? Careful: the obvious answer is wrong.

frames.check: Planning, not Analysis.
frames.teach: Five kinds: economic, organisational, technical, resource, schedule. The text elsewhere lists technical, economic, operational, legal and schedule, so give whichever list the question's wording is closer to and do not panic when the two disagree.
frames.ask: In this bank, which kind asks whether eleven branch managers will accept daily visibility of their loan book?

frames.check: Organisational feasibility.
frames.teach: That is the pattern for the whole answer: for each of the five, write one clause that names something in the scenario. A generic definition scores the definition mark and nothing else, and these questions are marked on the application.
frames.ask: One detail in the scenario tells you which fact finding techniques to use. Which detail, and which techniques?

frames.check: The managers cannot be away from their desks, so use questionnaires and sampling of existing documentation, with interviews kept for head office.
frames.teach: Answer the question that was asked, in the scenario's own nouns, and add the one line that shows judgement. That is the whole technique for Module One: it has no diagrams, so every mark is in naming the right thing and tying it to the words in front of you.

lockin.big: "Module One has no diagrams, so every mark is a named thing tied to a phrase in the scenario. Identify, justify, outline."
lockin.sub: Planning confirms feasibility. Analysis says WHAT, design says HOW. Stable requirements mean Waterfall, and changing ones mean Agile. Name the alternative you rejected, every time.
